rules.title: Ban on using or distributing common pricing algorithms to collude or coerce (AB 325)
rules.requirement: Landlords, property managers and software vendors may not use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm that uses competitor data to set or recommend rents or lease terms as part of an agreement to restrain trade. They also may not use or distribute one while pressuring others to adopt its recommended prices or terms. Renters harmed by algorithmic rent-fixing may report it to the Attorney General or sue under the Cartwright Act.
rules.key_value: Unlawful to use/distribute a common pricing algorithm (2+ users, competitor data) in restraint of trade, or to coerce adoption of its recommended price or commercial term
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies statewide to any person or business, including landlords and apartment rental companies, that uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm. That means a method or software used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or influence a price or commercial term. It covers all products and services, including residential rents. The ban is not limited to any class of buildings.
rules.exemptions: End consumers are not 'persons' under the section. According to a secondary source, single-firm algorithms that use only the business's own data are not covered.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.penalty: Cartwright Act remedies apply, and a violation is punishable as a crime. A secondary source adds amounts under SB 763 (Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 16755, 16755.1): criminal fines up to the greater of $6 million or twice the gain or loss for corporations, and up to the greater of $1 million or twice the gain or loss for individuals. AG or district attorney actions carry civil penalties up to $1 million. Private suits can recover treble damages, injunctive relief and attorneys' fees.

rules.title: 2024 California bill to ban pricing algorithms using competitors' nonpublic data (failed)
rules.requirement: A 2024 California bill would have banned pricing algorithms based on nonpublic data from competing companies. It did not advance and is not law.
rules.coverage_conditions: Would have applied statewide; no further details given.
rules.citation: Unnamed 2024 California bill (bill number not given)
rules.quoted_span: State lawmakers, however, failed to advance legislation last year "that would have banned the use of any pricing algorithms based on nonpublic data provided by competing companies," CalMatters reported.

rules.title: Application screening fee capped at actual costs and $30 (CPI-adjusted), with refund and availability limits
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge a screening fee only up to its actual out-of-pocket screening costs, and never more than $30 per applicant adjusted yearly for CPI since 1998 (listed as $68.96 for 2026). The landlord must give you an itemized receipt, refund any unused portion, and give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days. It cannot charge a fee if no unit is or will soon be available, and must either consider applications in the order received and approve the first qualified applicant, or refund the full fee to applicants not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of applying, whichever comes first.
rules.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted annually from 1998-01-01 ($68.96 for 2026 per Berkeley)
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property in California and their agents who charge rental applicants, including guarantors and cosigners, a fee to screen an application.
rules.exemptions: Under the first-come process, no refund is required for an applicant denied after consideration for failing the landlord's written screening criteria. Does not preempt deposit and fee rules under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act just cause for eviction and no-fault relocation assistance
rules.requirement: Once you have lived in your unit lawfully for 12 months, your landlord can end your tenancy only for a just cause listed in the law, and the written notice must state that cause. For a no-fault cause such as owner move-in, taking the unit off the market, or demolition or major remodel, the landlord must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your last month's rent.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months of tenancy; no-fault relocation = 1 month's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property in California, including mobilehome park units, once the tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the unit for 12 months. If an adult tenant is added before 24 months, it applies only when all tenants have occupied 12+ months or at least one has occupied 24+ months. Housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years is not covered (except mobilehomes). Does not apply where a qualifying local just cause ordinance (such as the Los Angeles JCO or RSO) covers the unit.
rules.exemptions: Transient or tourist hotels; nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended care and residential care facilities; school dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who lives there; owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADUs and JADUs); owner-occupied duplexes where the owner lived in one unit at the start of the tenancy (neither unit an ADU or JADU); housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the last 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable units (such as single-family homes or condos) not owned by a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member, if the tenant got the required written exemption notice; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners.
rules.interaction: Yields to BER-EVICT-01, LA-EVICT-01, LA-EVICT-02, SD-EVICT-01, SF-EVICT-01, SA-EVICT-01, SM-EVICT-01 where the local rule covers the unit.
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.penalty: A noncompliant termination notice is void. An owner who tries to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, attorney's fees and costs at the court's discretion, and up to three times actual damages plus punitive damages for willful conduct, oppression, fraud or malice. The Attorney General and the city attorney or county counsel may seek an injunction.

rules.title: Relocation payments for temporary capital improvement displacement under 20 days (San Francisco)
rules.requirement: If you must move out for less than 20 days for capital improvement work in San Francisco, your relocation payment is set by Civil Code § 1947.9 rather than the city's Rent Ordinance § 37.9C. For notices served March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, that is $446.00 per day per tenant household plus actual moving expenses.
rules.key_value: $446.00/day per household plus actual moving expenses (notices served 3/1/26–2/28/27)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants in San Francisco rent-controlled units temporarily displaced for less than 20 days for capital improvement work.
rules.quoted_span: The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.

rules.title: Housing Crisis Act relocation for lower-income households displaced by demolition
rules.requirement: If your protected unit is demolished for new housing and your household earns 80% of area median income or less, you must receive relocation benefits equal to those public entities pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. In Los Angeles, the owner pays the HCA amount or the city amount, whichever is higher.
rules.key_value: Relocation consistent with Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. for lower-income households
rules.coverage_conditions: Protected units demolished for new housing development; applies to lower-income occupants (80% AMI or below).
rules.quoted_span: 3. Pay relocation assistance to tenants in compliance with the State law’s Housing Crisis Act

rules.title: California statewide rent cap (Tenant Protection Act, AB 1482)
rules.requirement: In a covered unit, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus the local cost-of-living change, or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, and can raise it at most twice in 12 months. When a new tenancy starts, the landlord can set any starting rent, and the cap applies to increases after that.
rules.key_value: Lower of 5% + regional CPI or 10% per 12 months; at most 2 increases per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property in California, including mobilehome park units. It applies to rent increases on or after March 15, 2019 (February 18, 2021 for mobilehome tenancies). It does not cover housing that received its certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (rolling test), unless it is a mobilehome. It does not apply where a local rent control ordinance limits increases below this cap, such as the Los Angeles RSO. The section is set to be repealed on January 1, 2030.
rules.exemptions: Housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years. Deed-restricted, regulatory-restricted or subsidized affordable housing. School and university dormitories. Housing under local rent control that limits increases below this cap. Separately alienable units, such as single-family homes and condos, when the owner is not a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member and the tenant got the required written notice. Owner-occupied duplexes where the owner has lived in one unit since the start of the tenancy and neither unit is an ADU or JADU. Mobilehome homeowners.
rules.interaction: Yields to BER-RENT-01, LA-RENT-01, SF-RENT-01, SA-RENT-01, SM-RENT-01 where the local rule covers the unit.
rules.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower,
rules.penalty: The tenant can sue for injunctive relief, damages equal to the overcharge, and discretionary attorney's fees and costs. The tenant can recover up to three times the overcharge for willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct. The Attorney General and the city attorney or county counsel may also enforce. The statute of limitations is three years, and waivers are void.

rules.title: Limits on use of criminal history in tenant screening (FEHA / Civil Rights Council regulations)
rules.requirement: California landlords may not refuse everyone with a criminal record, and may not consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile records. If a landlord denies you because of a conviction, the conviction must be directly related to your ability to be a good tenant.
rules.key_value: No blanket criminal-record bans; arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged and juvenile records may not be considered
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers in California making rental decisions, including landlords and tenant screening companies, under FEHA regulations adopted by the Civil Rights Council (formerly the Fair Employment and Housing Council).
rules.exemptions: An owner who lives in the home and rents to one additional person is exempt from most FEHA rules.
rules.citation: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 2 (Civil Rights Council FEHA housing regulations); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
rules.quoted_span: Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.
rules.penalty: FEHA remedies: losses, injunction, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, attorney's fees.

rules.title: Source-of-income discrimination ban, including Section 8 and other housing vouchers, and credit-history alternative for subsidy holders (FEHA)
rules.requirement: A California landlord may not refuse to rent to you, set different terms or deposits, or advertise 'No Section 8' because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8, HUD-VASH and other housing subsidies. If you have a government rent subsidy, any income test must use only your share of the rent, and a landlord who checks credit must let you offer other proof that you can pay, such as benefit records, pay records or bank statements, and must reasonably consider it (SB 267, from January 1, 2024).
rules.key_value: Source of income, including Section 8 and VASH vouchers, is a protected class; subsidy holders may offer alternative evidence instead of credit history
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of any housing accommodation in California, including apartments, single-family homes, condos and subsidized housing. Also applies to property managers and tenant screening companies. 'Source of income' means lawful, verifiable income paid to the tenant, to the tenant's representative, or to the landlord on the tenant's behalf, including public assistance and housing subsidies. The credit-history and income-test rules apply when the applicant has a government rent subsidy.
rules.exemptions: An owner who lives in the home and rents to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but may not publish discriminatory advertisements. Asking about the level or source of income is not discrimination. Landlords may still verify employment, ask for landlord references and verify identity.
rules.quoted_span: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
rules.penalty: Enforced by the California Civil Rights Department. Remedies include out-of-pocket losses, injunctions, access to the denied housing, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney's fees. File with CRD within 1 year or in court within 2 years.

rules.title: California security deposit law: one-month cap, 21-day return and deduction limits
rules.requirement: Since July 1, 2024, a landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit (however labeled) of more than one month's rent on top of first month's rent; qualifying small landlords may take up to two months' rent. Within 21 days after you move out, the landlord must return the deposit or what remains of it, with an itemized statement, receipts, and (since April 1, 2025) photos for any deductions. The landlord may not deduct for ordinary wear and tear or preexisting damage, and no deposit may be called nonrefundable.
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent (2 months for qualifying small landlords); return within 21 days
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential rental security deposits in California, furnished or unfurnished. The one-month cap applies to security demanded or collected on or after July 1, 2024. Move-in photos are required for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025, and move-out/pre-repair photos since April 1, 2025. Electronic return applies from January 1, 2026 where the tenant paid deposit or rent electronically. A higher-than-standard deposit charged to a service member must be explained in writing and the extra returned within six months (from April 1, 2025). The landlord must give written notice of the tenant's right to a pre-move-out inspection, held no earlier than two weeks before move-out.
rules.exemptions: Small landlord exception to the one-month cap: a natural person (including a family trust) or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units offered for rent in total, may take up to two months' rent, but not from a service member. Advance payment of at least six months' rent is allowed on leases of six months or longer. Receipts are not required if repair and cleaning deductions total $125 or less, unless the tenant asks for them within 14 days. The inspection notice does not apply to terminations under CCP § 1161(2)-(4). Electronic return does not apply if the parties agreed in writing to another method.
rules.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
rules.penalty: Bad-faith retention or demand: statutory damages of up to twice the security plus actual damages; landlord forfeits any claim to the security for bad-faith noncompliance with the return requirements (§ 1950.5(h), (m)).

rules.requirement: This is a proposed Massachusetts House bill to prevent algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market. It is not law.

rules.title: Licensed broker fee disclosure to prospective tenants
rules.requirement: Only a licensed broker may charge a prospective tenant a fee for finding an apartment. At the first personal meeting, the broker must tell you in writing the fee amount, when and how it is paid, and whether it depends on a lease being signed.
rules.key_value: Written fee disclosure at first personal meeting; broker must be licensed
rules.coverage_conditions: Real estate brokers and salespeople who deal with prospective tenants in Massachusetts. The only source is secondary and does not cover the 2025 change on who pays the broker fee (see M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD1/2).
rules.quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.
rules.source_note: Secondary source fetched from the corpus link list; official text not in corpus.

rules.title: Broker fee paid only by the party that hired the broker
rules.requirement: A rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who first hired the broker under a contract. If the landlord or the landlord's agent hired the broker, you cannot be made to pay the broker fee.
rules.key_value: Broker fee paid only by the party that engaged the broker
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rentals in Massachusetts where a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is used to find a tenant or a rental unit.
rules.citation: M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD1/2 (as amended by St. 2025, c. 9, § 43)
rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

rules.title: Limit on up-front charges at start of tenancy (no application fees)
rules.requirement: At or before move-in, a Massachusetts landlord or the landlord's agent can only require first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, and the cost of buying and installing a new lock and key. Application fees, screening fees, and other up-front charges are not allowed, and neither is a broker fee paid to the landlord's agent.
rules.key_value: First month + last month + security deposit (≤1 month) + lock/key cost; nothing else
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential leases and tenancies in Massachusetts. Since the amendment effective August 1, 2025, the rule also covers agents of the landlord.
rules.exemptions: Leases or rentals of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes. Licensed real estate brokers may charge fees under separate rules (254 CMR 7; M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD1/2).
rules.quoted_span: (b) At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following:
rules.penalty: Damages. A secondary source cites Perry v. Equity Residential (2014), where a federal court awarded triple damages and attorney's fees for unlawful application fees.

rules.title: Ban on retaliatory termination, rent increase, or change in tenancy terms
rules.requirement: A landlord may not threaten or retaliate against you, for example with a termination notice, rent increase or major change in lease terms, because you reported code violations, took legal action under housing laws, complained in writing, or organized or joined a tenants' union. A termination notice (other than for nonpayment), a rent increase, or a major change in terms within six months of that activity is presumed to be retaliation, and you can recover 1 to 3 months' rent or your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees.
rules.key_value: 6-month rebuttable presumption of reprisal; damages of 1–3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants of residential premises in Massachusetts. Applies to any person or agent who threatens or takes reprisals.
rules.exemptions: Termination notices for nonpayment of rent do not trigger the presumption.
rules.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action
rules.penalty: Damages of at least one month's rent and up to three months' rent, or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Any lease waiver is void.

rules.title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control (M.G.L. c. 40P)
rules.requirement: Massachusetts cities and towns may not pass, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no state or local legal cap on rent increases in Massachusetts. A city or town that accepts Chapter 40P may adopt only a narrow, voluntary program in which the city pays owners the gap between market rent and controlled rent.
rules.key_value: Local rent control prohibited
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to every city and town in Massachusetts. The only local rent regulation allowed is the voluntary, city-compensated kind described in § 4(a) to (c).
rules.exemptions: A city or town that accepts Chapter 40P may adopt rent control only if: (a) owners may opt out after six months; (b) it does not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condo conversion or removal of units, and it does not apply to units of owners with fewer than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent over $400; and (c) the city pays owners the difference between market and controlled rent from its general funds.
rules.quoted_span: Section 4. No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:

rules.title: Initiative Petition 25-21: statewide cap on rent increases (blocked from the November 2026 ballot)
rules.requirement: This proposal would have limited yearly rent increases to the lower of CPI or 5% and repealed G.L. c. 40P. It is not law: on June 23, 2026 the SJC ruled it cannot appear on the November 2026 ballot because it includes a religious exemption.
rules.key_value: Lesser of CPI or 5% annually (proposed; not enacted)
rules.coverage_conditions: Would have applied to most residential rental units statewide.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units; new units less than 10 years old; certain publicly regulated units; short-term rentals; and units in facilities run only for educational, religious or nonprofit purposes.
rules.citation: Initiative Petition 25-21; Cella v. Attorney General, SJC-13893
rules.quoted_span: Under the proposed law, annual rent increases would have been limited to the lesser of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index or 5%.
rules.source_note: Secondary source fetched from the corpus link list; official text not in corpus.

rules.title: Massachusetts ban on source-of-income discrimination (public assistance and housing subsidies)
rules.requirement: A Massachusetts landlord may not refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because you receive public assistance or a housing subsidy such as a rental voucher. They also cannot do it because of the subsidy program's requirements.
rules.key_value: Source of income (public assistance, housing subsidies, rental assistance) is a protected class in rentals
rules.coverage_conditions: Any person furnishing rental accommodations in Massachusetts. The statute does not limit this to certain buildings.
rules.quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements

rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit law: one-month cap, separate bank account, interest, and 30-day return
rules.requirement: Your landlord cannot charge a security deposit of more than one month's rent, and must keep it in a separate interest-bearing account at a Massachusetts bank, giving you a receipt within 30 days and a written statement of the unit's condition within 10 days. The landlord must pay you 5% interest a year (or the lower rate the bank actually paid), and must return the deposit plus interest within 30 days after your tenancy ends, minus only allowed deductions backed by a sworn, itemized list.
rules.key_value: Max 1 month's rent; separate MA bank account; 5% annual interest (or the lower actual bank rate); return within 30 days; treble damages
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential tenancies in Massachusetts where the landlord collects a security deposit or last month's rent in advance. Interest on the security deposit is owed when the landlord holds it for one year or longer.
rules.exemptions: Leases or rentals of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes.
rules.quoted_span: a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3)
rules.penalty: If the landlord fails to put the deposit in a proper account, fails to return it within 30 days, or tries to enforce lease terms that conflict with the law, the landlord loses the right to keep any of it. The tenant can recover three times the deposit or balance owed, plus 5% interest, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 15B(6), (7)). If interest on last month's rent is not paid, the tenant can recover three times that interest plus costs and fees. If the yearly interest is not paid, the tenant may deduct it from the next rent payment.

rules.title: FAIR Act: ban on algorithmic rent-setting software that uses competitors' nonpublic data
rules.requirement: Starting July 1, 2027, New Jersey landlords may not pay for or use a 'coordinator': software or an algorithmic device that sets or recommends rents, lease terms or occupancy levels using competitors' nonpublic data. No one may perform a coordinating function or take part in parallel pricing coordination. Tenants can report violations through the Attorney General's complaint portal.
rules.key_value: Use of algorithmic rent-setting coordinators that use competitors' nonpublic data is banned from 2027-07-01; violations count as violations of the NJ Antitrust Act
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all owners of residential rental units in New Jersey and their agents, representatives and subcontractors, and also to software providers, coordinators and anyone else. Covers any house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit used as a primary residence. Building size and age do not limit coverage.
rules.exemptions: These are not coordinating functions: research or statistical use that is not used to set prices, free public rent estimates, real estate brokerage or listing databases that do not set or recommend prices, and government affordability controls. Simple non-AI spreadsheets that need human analysis and query-only databases are not algorithmic devices. Inpatient medical care, long-term care and detention facilities are excluded.
rules.conflict_note: Section 6(b) of the act bars municipalities from adopting ordinances that conflict with it. One member says local algorithmic-pricing ordinances in Jersey City, Hoboken or Newark could be preempted. The records here do not confirm what those ordinances say. Both sources give the same effective date, 2027-07-01, which comes from the July 20, 2026 approval date.
rules.penalty: A violation counts as a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act (P.L.1970, c.73), and the remedies of N.J.S.A. 56:9-6 through 56:9-17 apply. Complaints can be filed with the Attorney General.

rules.title: Residential rental application fee capped at $50 (CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A New Jersey landlord or their agent cannot charge more than $50 as an application or similar fee to rent or sublease a home; starting January 1, 2027 the cap is adjusted each year for inflation. If you are overcharged, you can report it to the Division of Consumer Affairs, and the overcharge is refunded to you from the penalty collected.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee; adjusted annually by CPI starting January 1, 2027 (increases only)
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords and their agents renting or subleasing residential rental property for dwelling purposes in New Jersey.
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units in one-family or two-family dwellings; New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees unless the licensee is the landlord.
rules.quoted_span:
shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
rules.penalty: Up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second, and $1,000 for each later offense, through summary proceedings under the Penalty Enforcement Law; the amount wrongfully charged is refunded to the applicant from the penalty.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act: good cause required to evict or refuse to renew
rules.requirement: Your landlord cannot evict you or refuse to renew your lease, written or oral, without one of the good causes listed in the law, such as nonpayment, disorderly conduct, damage, or breaking lease rules after a notice to stop. Each cause requires its own notice to quit, and lockouts or other self-help evictions are illegal. If you are evicted so the landlord can fix an illegal occupancy, the landlord must pay you relocation assistance equal to six months' rent.
rules.key_value: Listed good causes (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(a)-(r)), each with its own notice period from 3 days to 3 years; relocation assistance of 6 months' rent for evictions to correct illegal occupancy
rules.coverage_conditions: Most residential rentals, including apartment buildings, single-family homes, mobile homes and rooming houses. The relocation assistance covers tenants evicted under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(g)(3) to correct an illegal occupancy.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; transient or seasonal hotel and motel guests; units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member.
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a
rules.penalty: Treble damages plus attorney fees for false owner-occupancy claims or improper re-rental. Civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation for illegal residential use after a removal-from-market eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6). Unpaid relocation payments may be paid from a municipal relocation fund; where no fund exists, they accrue 18% annual interest and become a lien on the property.

rules.title: No statewide rent cap; increases must not be unconscionable and must follow local rent control
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no statewide rent cap, but any rent increase must not be unconscionable, must follow any local rent control ordinance, and can only take effect through a notice to quit and an offer of a new lease, not in the middle of a lease. If you think an increase is unconscionable, you can challenge it before a local rent board or in court.

rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protection Ordinance – just cause for eviction and no-fault relocation assistance
